title: Does Teacher Expertise Matter?
author: Paul A. Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Paul Kirschner and Nidhi Sachdeva, in the second post of a series on teacher expertise, ask why expertise is taken for granted in medicine, aviation and law but treated as optional in teaching. They argue that expertise is hidden in plain sight because expert teachers make the work look easy, and that great teaching is built on knowledge and judgment rather than charisma. They separate good teaching from expert teaching, saying experts see, notice and infer more, and that years of experience alone do not produce expertise. They name five pieces of expertise: deep domain knowledge, pattern recognition, rich mental models, deliberate practice and disciplined reflection. They close with an equity argument, that weak teaching costs most the pupils with the least home support, so expertise is a professional and moral necessity.
points: The authors distinguish experience from expertise, arguing that twenty years of repeated routines is not the same as organised, refined and reflected-upon experience.
Expert teaching is described as better noticing, since experts read ambiguous classroom signals such as silence or a correct answer more accurately than good teachers do.
Five named components (domain knowledge, pattern recognition, mental models, deliberate practice, reflection) give schools something concrete to develop.
The equity point is that the cost of merely adequate teaching falls hardest on pupils who cannot compensate at home.
quotes: Great teaching isn’t accidental, mystical, or reducible to charisma or other personality traits. It’s built on knowledge, judgment, and years of deliberately working on the gradual development of expertise.
Experience isn’t enough, it’s necessary but insufficient on its own. We often confuse experience with expertise, but they aren’t the same.
Expertise isn’t just accumulated time and speed/routine. It’s organised, refined, and reflected-upon experience.
Expert teachers don’t simply do the basics better. They see more, notice more, infer more, and respond more precisely.
The second is pattern recognition. Expert teachers are better at seeing what’s going on because they have better organised knowledge structures (i.e., cognitive schemata) in their long-term memory.
The fourth is deliberate practice. Expertise doesn’t develop through experience alone. It develops when teachers work consciously on getting better at specific aspects of practice.

That means the cost of ‘adequate’ isn’t evenly distributed. It falls most heavily on those least able to compensate for it. In other words: expertise isn’t a luxury or an optional extra for enthusiasts.
